facts.title: A triptych of paradise, pleasure, and punishment
facts.body: Bosch’s Garden of Earthly Delights (c. 1490–1500) opens from a gray Creation into Eden, a teeming garden of desire, and a dark musical hell. Few paintings invent a denser private cosmology.

facts.title: Eden before the fall’s full cost
facts.body: On the left God presents Eve to Adam in a landscape already seeded with odd creatures — innocence with a warning.

facts.title: The garden of myriad nudes
facts.body: The center panel swarms with naked figures, birds, and fruit. Readings range from moral satire to utopian fantasy; Bosch never captions his dream.

facts.title: Hell as broken instrument
facts.body: The right panel invents punishments from music, ice, and machinery — a night city of consequence.

facts.title: The pink fountain of life
facts.body: A fantastical pink structure rises at the garden’s axis — architecture that grows like a plant.

facts.title: The circular pool
facts.body: Figures bathe and ride beasts around a central pool — ritual or revel, depending on the viewer.

facts.title: Fruit larger than people
facts.body: Oversized berries and cherries dwarf the nudes. Desire is scaled until it becomes absurd.

facts.title: An owl in paradise
facts.body: Owls haunt Bosch’s Eden — vigilance, folly, or night watching day.

facts.title: Ears pierced by a knife
facts.body: In hell, a knife stands between severed ears — gossip and violence fused into one emblem.

facts.title: Adam and Eve in Eden
facts.body: In the left panel God presents Eve to Adam in a verdant Paradise filled with strange animals and a pink fountain — Bosch’s vision of creation before the Fall.
